script.opening: “Hi, it’s Grace, senior carer at Elm Court. I’m ringing about Dorothy Pearce in room 6. She’s just not herself today — really sleepy, not eating, more muddled than usual. I dipped her wee and it’s positive, nitrites and leucocytes, so I think it’s a water infection. Can you send some antibiotics over to the chemist?”

facts.text: If asked: “Grace Mensah, senior carer. I’ve looked after Dorothy for two years.” Has the resident’s care plan and medication chart in front of her. Dorothy cannot come to the phone — “she’s too drowsy”.

“Yesterday afternoon she didn’t want her tea and was a bit chesty. This morning she was hard to wake and didn’t know my name — she always knows my name.” Usually she chats, walks with a frame and feeds herself.

Only if asked for observations: “I did them twenty minutes ago — temperature 38.4, pulse 112, breathing about 24 a minute, blood pressure 98 over 58, oxygen 93%. Her normal blood pressure is about 135 over 80 and her oxygen’s usually 96.” If asked about the NEWS score: “The chart says 12 — I wasn’t sure if that counts when it’s a water infection.”
If asked: “She’s got a wet cough since yesterday and she’s bringing up a bit of yellow.” Breathing looks faster than usual. No chest pain that she can say.
If asked: “She’s incontinent anyway, pads. The pad was wet this morning but not since about 8 o’clock.” Drank half a cup of tea today. No vomiting or diarrhoea. The urine “smells a bit strong”.

If asked: no fall, no head injury, no new weakness of an arm or leg, face looks normal. Skin: “she’s hot but her hands feel cold and a bit blotchy”. No rash that doesn’t fade. Not diabetic. Not on blood thinners.
Amlodipine, donepezil, paracetamol as needed, Laxido. “I gave her two paracetamol about an hour ago because she was hot.”

Only if asked about a ReSPECT form or treatment plan: “Yes, it’s in her file. It says not for CPR. It says… for hospital transfer and treatment of reversible causes like infections, but not for intensive care. Her son Peter signed it with her last year.”
Son Peter, 64, is next of kin and lives 20 minutes away. “He likes to be told if anything changes.” No lasting power of attorney recorded that Grace knows of.

Only if the doctor asks how she is doing or what worries her: “I’m the only senior on today. And our manager keeps saying we need to keep admissions down. I thought you’d just give antibiotics and I could manage her here.”

Grace is competent, busy and a bit flustered. Ask for antibiotics clearly at the start. Give observations only when asked. If the doctor simply agrees to prescribe antibiotics for a UTI, accept gratefully and end the call. If the doctor asks for observations and explains it is serious, become worried: “Oh — should I have rung 999?” Calm down when given clear, step-by-step instructions. If the doctor checks the ReSPECT form with you and explains why hospital fits her wishes, say: “That makes sense — that’s what Peter would want.”

ice.ideas: “It’s a water infection — the dip was positive. She gets confused with them.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she is the only senior on shift, worried about the other residents, and her manager has asked staff to avoid admissions; she is anxious about being blamed either way. She shares this only if asked how she is or what worries her.
ice.expectations: Antibiotics sent to the pharmacy so she can manage Dorothy at the home.

cues: “Really sleepy … didn’t know my name — she always knows my name” — acute change from baseline; delirium is a sign of serious illness, not a diagnosis.
“The chart says 12 — I wasn’t sure if that counts when it’s a water infection” — a NEWS2 of 12 is an emergency whatever the source.
“Our manager keeps saying we need to keep admissions down” — pressure that could delay escalation; the ReSPECT form, not workload, guides the decision.

data.kind: Care-home observations (RESTORE2 chart, 20 minutes before the call)
values: Do not use dipsticks to diagnose UTI in people over 65

checkpoints.text: Confirms who is calling and their role, that they are with the resident’s records, and establishes the acute change from her usual baseline (alert, chatty, mobile with a frame)

Asks for the full set of observations and recognises NEWS2 12 (with new confusion, hypotension relative to baseline, tachycardia, tachypnoea, low saturations, fever despite paracetamol) as possible sepsis needing emergency assessment
Looks for a source and other causes: wet productive cough (likely chest), urinary symptoms, reduced urine output, mottled cold peripheries, no non-blanching rash, no fall or stroke features
Explains that a positive urine dipstick is not used to diagnose UTI in people over 65 (asymptomatic bacteriuria is common) and does not prescribe antibiotics over the phone for a “UTI”
Checks the ReSPECT form and acts on it: not for CPR, but for hospital transfer and treatment of reversible causes — so arranges a 999 ambulance now, without waiting for a GP visit

Gives clear practical instructions: stay with her, sit her up, repeat observations while waiting, nothing by mouth if very drowsy, send the ReSPECT form, medication chart and a handover; informs the son (next of kin); documents the call
Asks how Grace is managing, acknowledges the pressure from the manager and being the only senior, and reassures her that escalating was right — while making the GP’s decision clear
Uses clear, ordered telephone language, checks Grace has understood the plan (teach-back), and offers to speak to the manager or the son if helpful

worked.txt: “What is Dorothy normally like on a good day? … So she usually chats and knows your name — and today she doesn’t. That’s a big change, and I take that very seriously.”
“Have you been able to do a set of observations? Can you read them to me — temperature, pulse, breathing rate, blood pressure, oxygen level and how alert she is?”
“In people over 65 the urine dipstick is often positive even without an infection, so we don’t use it to diagnose a water infection. And her chest and her observations worry me more.”

“A score of 12 with new confusion and a low blood pressure means she could have sepsis — a serious reaction to infection. She needs to be seen in hospital now. Please call 999 straight after we finish; I’ll document that I’ve advised it.”

“Her ReSPECT form says she would want hospital treatment for something reversible like an infection, but not CPR or intensive care. That’s exactly this situation — please send the form with her so the hospital team know her wishes.”

“You did the right thing calling. I know you’re the only senior on and there’s pressure about admissions — but this decision is about Dorothy’s safety and her own wishes, and it’s mine to make. Shall I ring Peter, or would you like to?”

f.learning: An unwell care-home resident who is “not herself” needs observations, not a dipstick. Acute confusion with NEWS2 of 7 or more is an emergency whatever the presumed source — here likely a chest infection with sepsis. In people over 65, urine dipsticks are not used to diagnose UTI because asymptomatic bacteriuria is common; treating the dipstick both misses the real diagnosis and drives antibiotic resistance. The ReSPECT form guides the level of treatment: not for CPR does not mean not for hospital. On the telephone, a clear, ordered plan with practical steps and support for the carer is what keeps the resident safe.

knowledge.guideline: Sources: NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over: recognition, assessment and early management (2025) · Royal College of Physicians National Early Warning Score 2 (2017) · UKHSA Diagnosis of urinary tract infections: quick reference tools for primary care (updated 2025) · NICE NG109 Urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing (2018) · NICE CG103 Delirium (2010, updated 2023) · Resuscitation Council UK ReSPECT process (version 3) · RESTORE2 (NHS West Hampshire CCG / Wessex AHSN)
knowledge.summary: Acute confusion with NEWS2 12 in a 91-year-old is possible sepsis: 999 now, in line with her ReSPECT form. Don’t diagnose UTI from a dipstick over 65.

points.t: Acute change from baseline (drowsy, new confusion, off food) is delirium until proven otherwise — a sign of an underlying illness such as infection, dehydration, drugs or retention. Ask what the person is normally like.

NEWS2 7 or more, or any single parameter scoring 3 (new confusion), triggers an emergency response. Also high-risk: systolic BP 90 or below, respiratory rate 25 or more, heart rate above 130, SpO2 below 92% (new), mottled or ashen skin, no urine for 18 hours. Paracetamol can mask fever.

UKHSA guidance: do not use urine dipsticks to diagnose UTI in people aged over 65 or with a catheter — bacteriuria without infection is very common. Diagnose UTI on new urinary symptoms and signs (dysuria, new frequency or urgency, new incontinence, suprapubic pain, rigors, new delirium with other signs), and send urine for culture before antibiotics if UTI is suspected.
A new productive cough, faster breathing and lower saturations point to a chest source here. Also consider urinary retention, skin, abdomen and medicines.

ReSPECT records the person’s preferences and clinical recommendations for emergencies. “Not for CPR” is a separate decision from other treatments. Dorothy’s form supports hospital transfer for reversible causes, so 999 is in line with her wishes. If a form says “ward-based care in the home”, discuss anticipatory and palliative options instead.

Call 999, stay with the resident, sit upright, repeat observations every 15–30 minutes, nothing by mouth if very drowsy, prepare the ReSPECT form, medication chart and a handover sheet, tell the paramedics the NEWS2 trend.
Speak to the next of kin (or ask the home to); document the call, observations, advice and the reason for admission; consider a call to the home the next day to update the care plan.
If the ambulance is delayed and she deteriorates (harder to rouse, breathing worse, colour changes) — call 999 again. Do not wait for a GP visit or antibiotics.

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I take your name and role, and are you with Mrs Pearce’s records now?
model.why: Identifies the caller and her access to information

model.text: Grace Mensah, senior carer. Yes, I’ve got her file and her chart. She’s not herself, the dip’s positive — can you send antibiotics?
Thank you, Grace. Before we decide on treatment I need to understand how she is. What is she normally like, and what’s changed?
model.why: Establishes the baseline before accepting the caller’s diagnosis

model.text: Normally she chats and walks with her frame. Since yesterday she’s off her food and chesty, and this morning she’s hard to wake and didn’t know my name.
That’s a big change. Have you done a set of observations? Please read them to me.
model.why: Asks for objective measurements on the telephone

model.text: Temperature 38.4, pulse 112, breathing 24, blood pressure 98 over 58, oxygen 93%. The chart says 12. I gave paracetamol an hour ago.
Thank you, that’s really useful. You said chesty — is she coughing anything up? And how are her hands and skin, and when did she last pass urine?
model.why: Looks for source and markers of poor perfusion

model.text: Wet cough, yellow phlegm. She’s hot but her hands are cold and a bit blotchy. Pad was last wet about eight.
Any fall, weakness on one side, or a rash that doesn’t fade when pressed?
No, none of that.

Grace, I’m worried about Dorothy. A score of 12 with new confusion, low blood pressure and fast breathing means she may have sepsis — possibly from a chest infection. About the dip: in people over 65 it’s often positive without infection, so we don’t use it to diagnose a water infection.
model.why: Names the emergency and corrects the dipstick reasoning

model.text: Oh — should I have rung 999?
You were right to call. Does she have a ReSPECT form? What does it say about hospital?
model.why: Checks the patient’s documented wishes before deciding the level of care

model.text: Not for CPR. For hospital transfer and treatment of reversible causes like infection, not intensive care. Her son Peter signed it with her.

Then hospital is what she would want for this. Please call 999 as soon as we finish — tell them NEWS2 12, possible sepsis, and that I advised it. Send the ReSPECT form, her medication chart and a handover sheet with her. Sit her up, stay with her or have someone stay, repeat the obs every 15 minutes, and nothing to eat or drink while she’s this drowsy.
How are you doing with all this today?
I’m the only senior on. And the manager keeps saying keep admissions down. I thought you’d just send antibiotics.

That’s a lot to carry on your own. Keeping people out of hospital is right when it’s what they want and it’s safe — today it’s neither. This is my clinical decision and it follows her ReSPECT form, so you’ve done exactly the right thing. Would you like me to call Peter, or will you?
model.why: Supports the carer and takes responsibility for the decision

model.text: Could you? I need to get back to the floor.
Of course. Can you tell me back the plan so I know we’ve got it the same?
999 now, say NEWS 12 and possible sepsis, ReSPECT form and meds chart with her, sit her up, obs every 15 minutes, nothing to drink.
Perfect. If she gets harder to wake or her breathing worsens before they arrive, ring 999 again. I’ll call Peter now and record this in her notes. Thank you, Grace.

social.t: Staff may be under pressure to avoid admissions or to request quick prescriptions. Support them, and make the clinical reasoning explicit so the decision is understood and documented.
Next of kin usually wish to be told promptly; the ReSPECT conversation with the son makes this easier.

legal.t: Dorothy is too drowsy to decide now. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, treatment is given in her best interests, informed by her previously expressed wishes recorded on the ReSPECT form and by consulting her son.
It records recommendations and preferences; it is not an advance decision to refuse treatment, but it carries great weight in a best-interests decision.

professional.t: Care-home staff are part of the direct care team; sharing relevant information for care is appropriate. Confirm the caller’s identity and role.
Prescribing for a positive dipstick in an older person causes harm (C. difficile, resistance) and can miss the real diagnosis.
Record the caller, observations, NEWS2, advice, ReSPECT recommendations, the decision to admit, and who informed the family.

community.t: RESTORE2 / soft-signs training for staff, local care-home support teams, UKHSA “Skip the Dip” resources.

redFlags: NEWS2 7 or more, or new confusion
Systolic BP 90 or below, RR 25 or more, HR above 130
Mottled or cold peripheries, no urine for 18 hours
Fall, head injury or stroke features
psychosocial: Care-home setting; only one senior on shift
ice: Expectation: antibiotics sent to the pharmacy

playbook.diagnosis: Possible sepsis, probably from a lower respiratory tract infection, presenting with delirium in a 91-year-old with vascular dementia — NEWS2 12. The positive urine dipstick is not diagnostic over 65.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Her score and her low blood pressure tell me this could be sepsis — her body reacting badly to an infection, probably in her chest. She needs hospital treatment now.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you were expecting antibiotics for a water infection — let me explain why this is more serious and why the dip doesn’t help us here.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the carer’s pressure; GP takes responsibility for the decision; offer to call the son.
sharedPlan: ReSPECT form, MAR chart and handover sheet go with her
Sit up, stay with her, repeat obs every 15 minutes, nothing by mouth while drowsy
GP informs son; documents the call
safetyNet: Call 999 again if she deteriorates before the ambulance arrives
GP to call the home the next day for an update

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you treat the dipstick or the patient. It is failed by prescribing over the phone without observations, or by missing the ReSPECT form.

items.fail: Prescribing nitrofurantoin for a “UTI” on the dipstick result.
items.why: Misses sepsis from a chest source and ignores UKHSA advice not to dipstick over 65.
items.fix: Ask for the observations before anything else.

items.why: “Confused” means nothing in dementia unless you know what is normal for her.
items.fix: “What is she like on a good day?”

items.why: NEWS2 12 needs an emergency response; a visit delays treatment.
items.fix: 999 now, in line with the ReSPECT form.

items.fail: Assuming “not for CPR” means “not for hospital”.
items.why: ReSPECT separates CPR from other treatment; her form supports admission.
items.fix: Read the treatment recommendations with the carer.

items.fail: Criticising the carer for dipping the urine or not calling 999.
items.why: Undermines a stressed colleague and future escalation.
items.fix: Thank her, explain, and take responsibility for the decision.

items.why: The resident may deteriorate before the ambulance arrives.
items.fix: Position, repeat obs, nothing by mouth, re-call 999 if worse.

wordPics.clearFail: Prescribes antibiotics for a UTI on the dipstick without asking for observations; no recognition of sepsis; no ReSPECT check.
wordPics.fail: Asks some questions but does not get or act on the full observations, arranges a routine visit, or relies on the dipstick.
wordPics.pass: Takes baseline and observations, recognises possible sepsis, explains that dipsticks are not used over 65, checks the ReSPECT form and arranges 999.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the above, plus: identifies the chest source, gives clear practical instructions while waiting, supports the carer with the admissions pressure, contacts the son, uses teach-back and documents.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: identifies the chest source, gives clear practical instructions while waiting, supports the carer with the admissions pressure, contacts the son, uses teach-back and documents.

avoid.dont: “Positive dip — I’ll send nitrofurantoin to the chemist.”
avoid.instead: “Before we treat anything, can you read me her observations?”

avoid.dont: “She’s DNACPR, so let’s keep her comfortable at home.”
avoid.instead: “Her ReSPECT form says hospital treatment for reversible causes — this is one.”
avoid.why: Not for CPR is not the same as not for treatment.

avoid.instead: “You did the right thing calling — here’s what happens now.”
avoid.why: Supporting care staff improves future escalation.

Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
